title: Making the EU’s new industrial rulebook work for Central Europe
gist: EU capitals are abandoning old trade-policy battle lines as China Shock 2.0 hits, with Berlin warming to cross-sector protections and Warsaw now backing CBAM. CEE faces industrial power prices far above China and the US and has little fiscal space, so the author urges it to shape the Industrial Accelerator Act, CBAM extension, steel-style safeguards, a possible 'European 301' and the 2028 EU budget so that reshoring lands in its factories.

insights.claim: Berlin is coming to appreciate the need for cross-sector protections against Chinese overcapacity, Paris is avoiding gloating about strategic autonomy, and the Tusk government has switched Warsaw to outward support for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
insights.so_what: Broadening political coalition makes tougher EU trade defense against China more likely in coming months.
insights.quote: capitals are already abandoning familiar positions and old battle lines
insights.locator: European manufacturing hubs don’t need to agree
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Upcoming EU policy initiatives are unlikely to address CEE's complaint that Green Deal mandatory decarbonization targets undermined competitiveness.
insights.so_what: Do not expect a rollback of core decarbonization rules; adjustment comes through trade tools instead.
insights.locator: For Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), these shifts
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: EU industrial electricity averaged €0.199/kWh in 2024 versus €0.082 in China and €0.075 in the United States.
insights.so_what: A ~2.5x power-cost gap structurally handicaps energy-intensive EU manufacturing.
insights.locator: To a degree, the numbers back them up
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Between 2019 and 2023 industrial electricity prices rose 171 percent in Hungary and 137 percent in Poland, versus 21 percent in the United States.
insights.so_what: CEE has fared worse than the EU average on energy costs, eroding its low-cost manufacturing advantage.
insights.locator: To a degree, the numbers back them up
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: CEE labor costs are now much higher than in China and in countries like Morocco that have favorable EU trade agreements and substantial Chinese investment.
insights.so_what: Morocco is emerging as a competing near-shore platform, including for Chinese capital targeting the EU market.
insights.locator: To a degree, the numbers back them up
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: CEE capitals have less fiscal space and borrow at higher rates than Western member states; Poland and Romania, despite high growth and less reliance on Germany, have high and growing deficits that limit investment in reshoring infrastructure and subsidies.
insights.so_what: Fiscal constraints mean CEE cannot win a national subsidy race against France, Germany or Italy.
insights.locator: Just as concerning is the fact
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Tariffs, taxes and subsidies will not suffice without private investment, but private capital is unlikely to bet on European manufacturing without an economic security mandate providing a floor in the market.
insights.so_what: Policy-driven floors (local content, safeguards) are a precondition for private manufacturing capex in Europe.
insights.quote: Without an economic security mandate providing a floor in the market, would global private capital really bet on manufacturing in Europe now?
insights.locator: Just as concerning is the fact
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

themes.theme: Industrial Accelerator Act and Made in Europe

insights.claim: The Industrial Accelerator Act, in early legislative stages, would turn the February 2025 Clean Industrial Deal into binding rules, including local content requirements for public tenders and subsidies and onshoring commitments for screened foreign investors.
insights.so_what: Binding local-content rules would favor EU-based manufacturers in public procurement and subsidy schemes.
insights.locator: The Industrial Accelerator Act, which is currently
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The act was originally called the 'Industrial Decarbonization Accelerator Act'; dropping 'Decarbonization' captures the shift of the policy debate from climate toward industrial security.
insights.so_what: Signals EU priority shifting from decarbonization to competitiveness and security.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: CEE fears new rules will raise costs for its producers without guaranteeing demand, because fiscally stronger states can pair national procurement preferences with subsidies, and CEE lacks large corporations to lobby in Brussels as France, Germany and Italy have.
insights.so_what: Benefits of EU industrial policy may accrue to large Western member states and their national champions.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: A solution could be loosening 'Made in Europe' to 'Made with Europe', bringing trusted trading partners into the network, and updating competition rules to stop large states from reserving national subsidies for national firms.
insights.so_what: A 'Made with Europe' standard would widen eligibility to allied-country suppliers.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The coming year will see steps toward implementing CBAM, more frequent use of safeguards and a growing debate over a 'European 301' that could allow a blanket tariff on Chinese goods.
insights.so_what: A blanket EU tariff tool on China is now in mainstream debate — material tail risk for Chinese exporters to Europe.
insights.locator: CEE will also need a stronger position
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Warsaw supports the Commission's December 2025 proposal to extend CBAM to some 180 downstream products from 2028, which would help mid-stream CEE manufacturers whose imported inputs are currently subject to CBAM while finished goods are not.
insights.so_what: Downstream CBAM extension closes a loophole penalizing EU mid-stream producers versus finished-goods imports.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The EU's new steel regulation halves import quotas and doubles out-of-quota duties to 50 percent; other metal inputs will be considered next, but this approach is unlikely to extend to consumer goods because it affects all trade partners.
insights.so_what: Supportive for EU steel producers; aluminum and downstream steel are candidate next targets.
insights.quote: The new steel regulation halves quotas and doubles out-of-quota duties to 50 percent.
insights.locator: While the debate over a European 301
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Positions on cross-sector China tariffs vary: Warsaw is hawkish, Prague would be too were it not for its car industry, and Hungary remains highly skeptical despite this year's change in government.
insights.so_what: CEE remains split, but could trade support for an incremental European 301 for guarantees that Western firms buy from CEE producers.
insights.locator: While the debate over a European 301
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: In negotiations on the seven-year EU budget from 2028, innovation and clean tech must compete with defense projects and Ukraine support, and cohesion and CAP spending are being folded into a single National and Regional Partnership Plan.
insights.so_what: Competition for EU funds threatens traditional cohesion flows to CEE.
insights.locator: The coming months will be crucial
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: A minority of member states including Austria rule out any EU budget increase, political uncertainty in France and Germany means no guaranteed broker, and Czechia is on the cusp of becoming a net budget contributor.
insights.so_what: Risk that CEE loses out on EU investment in energy and transport infrastructure.
insights.locator: Despite the mushrooming of new roles
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Central Europe's united front at the February Competitiveness Council achieved meager results — only slightly longer ETS free allocations — so CEE should stop treating protectionism and competitiveness as opposing camps and use support for Franco-German-aligned measures to secure regional benefits.
insights.so_what: Expect CEE to shift from deregulation demands toward bargaining inside a more protectionist EU framework.
insights.quote: The task, then, is not to choose between protectionism and competitiveness but to write the rules
insights.locator: The united front displayed by Central Europe
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
